name: Flat cap

card.summary: The flat cap is a rounded wool or tweed cap with a short stiff brim, worn to add a classic, put-together finish to an outfit and to cover or frame the hairline.
card.aka: paddy cap; scally cap; cabbie cap; driving cap; ivy cap; bunnet; sixpence
card.note: A small brim gives little sun protection for the face.

quick.overview:
A flat cap is a rounded hat with a low crown and a small, stiff brim at the front, usually in tweed, wool or cotton. It dates to 16th-century Northern England and has been worn across Britain and Ireland ever since.

In style terms it adds a vintage, polished look and can frame the face and hide a receding or thinning hairline while worn. It has a long list of regional names, from paddy cap to scally cap.
quick.how: People wear it in place of a baseball cap, matching it with jackets, knitwear or casual outfits. It is made in tweed, wool, cotton, corduroy, linen or leather and is chosen to fit the head closely.
quick.risks: A dermatology study found that small-brimmed hats, including the flat cap, give negligible sun protection except at the vertex and forehead. Wide brims are needed for cheeks and nose.

lead: The flat cap is a rounded cap with a small, stiff brim at the front, usually in tweed, wool or cotton, though leather, linen and corduroy are also used.[1] It emerged in 16th-century Northern England, where it was usually called a bonnet, and an English law of 1571 required most non-noble men to wear woollen caps on Sundays and holidays.[1]

As a style item it gives a vintage silhouette and frames the upper face. It is known by many names, including paddy cap in Ireland, bunnet in Scotland, scally cap, cabbie cap, golf cap and ivy cap.[1][2] Notable wearers listed by Wikipedia include David Beckham, AC/DC singer Brian Johnson and the poet Pablo Neruda.[1]

A 1992 study in the British Journal of Dermatology measured how well hats protect different parts of the head. It reported that small-brimmed hats such as the flat cap protected only the vertex and forehead, while a brim wider than 7.5 cm was needed for reasonable protection of the nose and cheeks.[3]

angle.text: The cap adds a classic, deliberate look to an outfit and covers the hair while worn. Its low profile sits close to the head and frames the forehead.

paras: The flat cap has a rounded crown that sits low on the head and a small stiff peak. The crown is built from fabric panels and typically lined inside for comfort.[1][2] It differs from the newsboy cap, which has a fuller crown made from more panels.[2]

The style dates from the 16th century and spread across Britain and Ireland in the 19th and early 20th centuries. It also reached southern Italy, Turkey, where it replaced the fez, the Balkans and Madrid.[1] Grokipedia adds that it became associated with working-class dress and later with golf and country pursuits.[2]
No studies found on its appearance effects. A 1992 measurement study of sun protection found small-brimmed hats such as the flat cap gave negligible protection across most of the face.[3]

timeline.event: The style appears in Northern England as a bonnet.[1]
English law requires most non-noble men to wear woollen caps on Sundays and holidays.[1]
